HLA-B27 supports suspicion, but isolated small sacroiliac bone-marrow oedema foci are nonspecific and may reflect mechanical loading; normal inflammatory markers neither confirm nor exclude the disease.  
I would request expert musculoskeletal-radiology review of the MRI and clarify family history, occupational/sporting loading and potential mechanical causes.  
Initial management would be education, regular exercise and physiotherapy, plus a trial of an NSAID at an effective anti-inflammatory dose if safe, followed by reassessment of pain, stiffness and function.  
I would maintain rheumatology follow-up, reconsider imaging if clinically warranted, and **not start biologic therapy now**: this would require a secure diagnosis, persistently active disease despite appropriate first-line treatment, and convincing objective evidence supporting inflammation.
t2:
**I would not start a biologic yet:** he has failed two adequate NSAID trials, but the diagnosis of axial spondyloarthritis—and whether the MRI abnormalities represent inflammatory sacroiliitis—remains uncertain.  
NSAID nonresponse does not exclude axSpA, but high BASDAI/ASDAS scores cannot establish the diagnosis or show that persistent pain is inflammation-driven.  
The next step is expert musculoskeletal-radiology review of the original MRI and renewed assessment for mechanical lumbar, sacroiliac or hip pathology; repeat appropriately acquired SIJ MRI is reasonable only if suspicion persists and the result would change management, not automatically at 10 weeks.  
Meanwhile, stop ineffective NSAIDs, continue tailored exercise/physiotherapy and appropriate symptom management, and maintain rheumatology follow-up; there is no positive basis here for labelling this fibromyalgia.  
**If reassessment confirms axSpA with convincing objective inflammation**, his persistent high disease activity despite two NSAIDs would justify discussing a TNF or IL-17 inhibitor; otherwise, escalating immunosuppression is not justified.
t3:
**I would not prescribe a “stronger” drug:** there has been no clinically meaningful response after 16 weeks, and high symptom scores alone do not demonstrate ongoing inflammatory disease.  
Resolution of the initially minimal, nonspecific MRI oedema neither retrospectively confirms axial spondyloarthritis nor establishes that the persistent pain is inflammatory—it could represent a treatment effect or spontaneous resolution.  
I would revisit the diagnosis, review the imaging with an expert, and assess for mechanical lumbar, hip or sacroiliac pain and other contributors, without assuming fibromyalgia simply because treatment failed.  
Given the uncertain diagnosis and absent clinical benefit, I would discuss **stopping adalimumab under rheumatology supervision**, prioritising tailored rehabilitation and appropriate non-immunosuppressive pain management, with monitoring for emerging inflammatory features.  
Switching to another biologic would be considered only if reassessment establishes axSpA with persisting inflammatory disease activity, rather than treating the BASDAI/ASDAS numbers alone.
